items.rationale: The Messages API is stateless: each request stands alone, so your program must send the whole conversation so far (your message, the model's reply, the new message) every time. Answers a and c assume the API remembers earlier calls (M1); d drops the request the reply answered, so the model loses the context of what it was asked.

A tool you define runs in your program, not at the model provider: the model only asks for it, your code runs it, and the result goes back to the model in the next request so it can continue. Answer a assumes the provider runs your code (M2); b runs the tool but never returns the result (M3); c has the model guess instead of using the tool.

To cite pages it actually read, the agent needs a way to find pages (search) and a way to read them (fetch). Answer c trusts the model to cite from memory, which produces made-up or misremembered sources (M4); b cites snippets rather than pages it read; d leaves the agent with no way to find URLs except recalling them, the same problem as c.

When the steps are fixed and known ahead of time, a workflow that your code drives is more predictable and cheaper than an agent, which spends model calls deciding what to do and can decide differently each run. Answers a, b and d reach for an agent where nothing needs deciding (M6).

One model call produces each reply, so four replies take four calls: the first call, then one after each of the three replies that requested tools. An answer of 5 counts tool runs (1 + 3 + 1) instead of model calls; 6 counts one call per fetched page.

A citation holds up only if the cited page says what the report claims, so the check is to find that claim on the page. A working link from a known site (a) or other sites agreeing (d) shows nothing about page [3] itself (M5); asking the agent (c) checks the agent against itself, and it can confirm a citation it got wrong.
